vignette:
She is nineteen years old, though she carries herself like someone much older. The first time she came into the clinic, her hands were still raw from hauling nets the night before—salt-crusted, calloused, trembling slightly as she tucked them under her thighs. She is a fisherman, like her father and his father before him, and she works the morning tide out of a small village on the Atoll’s leeward side. Her boyfriend, also a fisherman, rides in the same skiff. They have been together since she was sixteen, and he is the only person who knows the full weight of what she carries.

The thing that broke her happened eighteen months ago, in the shallow lagoon just beyond the reef. She had been out with her uncle and two cousins, hauling in a night’s catch under a half-moon. The weather was calm, the water clear enough to see the coral below. They were laughing about something—she cannot remember what—when her cousin, a boy of fourteen, stood up too quickly to reach for a line. The skiff tipped. Not badly, not dangerously, but enough that he lost his footing and slid over the gunwale. She saw it happen. He hit the water, came up sputtering, laughing, waving a hand. And then the current took him. It was not a dramatic wave or a shark—just the undertow that runs along the outer drop-off. He was gone before she could even call his name. They found his body two days later, tangled in the mangrove roots on the far side of the island.

She does not talk about that night. She cannot. Whenever she tries, her chest tightens, and the words catch in her throat like fish bones. But the images come anyway—without warning, without mercy. She will be standing at the cleaning table, knife in hand, gutting a tuna, and suddenly she sees her cousin’s face, his open mouth, the dark water closing over his head. The smell of the ocean, which she once loved, now makes her nauseous. She has stopped eating fish. She avoids the village wharf. Her boyfriend has started taking the boat out alone, because when she steps onto the deck, her legs go weak and she has to sit down. She used to be the strongest of her crew. Now she cannot even stand the sound of water lapping against the hull at night. She sleeps with the windows shut, a fan running, to drown it out.

Her relationship is strained. Her boyfriend is patient, but she knows he is tired. She snaps at him for no reason—when he comes home smelling of salt, when he laughs too loud, when he looks at her with that worried, searching expression. She knows he loves her. She also knows she is pushing him away, and she cannot stop. At night she has dreams where she is underwater, lungs burning, and she wakes up gasping, drenched in sweat. Sometimes she does not wake up at all—she just lies there, frozen, listening to her own heartbeat, convinced that if she closes her eyes again she will see the boy’s hand disappearing beneath the surface.

She stopped going to church. The pastor’s voice reminds her of the prayers they said at the funeral. She cannot look at the ocean without feeling that pull, that cold certainty that it is only a matter of time before it takes someone else. She grips the armrest of the chair in my office as she tells me this, knuckles white. She is here because her grandmother insisted. But she does not believe talking will fix anything. She just wants the images to stop. She wants to be able to stand on her own boat again. She wants to sleep without seeing that hand, still reaching, still reaching, as the water swallowed him whole.
